title: The Lamp on the Hill
paragraphs: If we were to establish a garden, we should decide which trees and flowers should adorn it, think of and implement the amenities needed for the comfort of those who come for a stroll and also carefully avoid things which should not find a place in the garden.

Since the establishment of a garden can have parallels with the making of a book, a verse in Tolkāppiyam throws light on the defects to be avoided in a book. Traffic rules prescribe whether we should keep to the right or the left though it differs from country to country. Although this is an important issue, even more important is the fact that without obtaining the permission or observing the signal one should not cross the road.

In the same manner, though a swimming pool is essential in a park, one should not dig a deep well in another corner of the park. The reason is that children who come to the park, accompanied by their parents, should not fall into the well by accident.

A few would come to the garden holding a book with the intention of reading it there. For their sake, bright lamps should burn in a few places. In the same way, lamps should not be there in places where men and women can relax enjoying privacy which is necessary after a day’s work. If light is required there it should be dim.
Though the toilet is essential to answer the call of nature, it should not be constructed in the centre of the park.
Such dos and don’ts are in order in a book too, which the following verse lists:

> A study sharp-eyed > Points to defects that stain a composition: > Tautology, inconsistency, understatement, > Overstatement, verbiage, obscurity, > Cacophony, contemptible things in unworthy diction, > Persisting in one’s own pet ideas, > Incomprehensibility of varied sorts > And failings that issue from these.

Tautology is saying the same thing again which is unnecessary. Inconsistency is saying things which are contradictory to one another. Understatement refers to making something seem less important or less impressive than it really is. Overstatement is its opposite. Verbiage is the use of too many words or of more difficult words than needed to express an idea. Obscurity is being difficult to understand. Cacophony is a mixture of loud unpleasant sounds. Such of these defects will not add to the worth of a book.
A book free from these shortcomings will be like the bright lamp on a hillock enlightening minds. Now what are the features of excellence of a composition?
> Brevity and perspicuousness, > Pleasing, worthy diction, > Pleasing sounds, > Depth of thought and ideas, > Right organization, > Acceptability in a large measure, > Sublimity > And coherence.
